lead: A program often has to choose one action from several. Python does this with conditional statements: if, if-else and if-elif-else. Each condition is a boolean expression that is either True or False. Python tests conditions in the order written and runs only the first block whose condition is True. This is how marks become grades, UPI payments pass or fail checks, and a login form rejects a wrong password. The rule is simple: colon ends the test line, indentation marks the block, and the first true branch wins.
prereq: You need: booleans, comparison operators and indentation from Unit 1.

sections.h3: The if statement chooses one block

blocks.text: An if statement has three parts: the keyword if, a condition, and a colon. The condition is a boolean expression, such as marks >= 75. The colon ( : ) marks the start of the block. The block is written below, indented by four spaces. Python runs the block only when the condition is True. When it is False, Python skips the whole indented block.

Comparison operators make conditions: < (less than), <= (less than or equal), > (greater than), >= (greater than or equal), == (equal) and != (not equal). The operator = assigns a value; == compares two values. Boolean operators combine tests: and is true only when both sides are true, or is true when at least one side is true, and not reverses True to False. For example, marks >= 60 and marks <= 75 is true for 70.

Indentation is not decoration. In Python, the same indentation groups statements into one block. A missing or extra space changes the meaning or raises IndentationError. The condition line always ends with a colon. The next line must be indented more than the if line.

An if-else statement gives two paths. The if block runs when the condition is True; the else block runs when it is False. else has no condition but does need a colon. Write else: and an indented block. Only one of the two blocks runs.

When there are more than two paths, use if-elif-else. elif means else if, and carries its own condition and colon. Python checks the if condition first, then each elif from top to bottom. The first True condition runs its block; all later tests are skipped. If no condition is True, the else block runs. else is optional, but it catches the remaining case.

Order matters because the first true branch wins. Suppose marks = 78 and the tests are marks >= 90, then marks >= 75, then marks >= 60. Test 1: 78 >= 90 is False. Test 2: 78 >= 75 is True. Python runs Grade B and does not test 78 >= 60. If the 75 test came before the 90 test, a mark of 95 would wrongly get B, so lower cut-offs must come after higher cut-offs.

You can nest an if inside another if's block; Python places no limit on depth, but keep nesting shallow because deep nesting is hard to read. Example: inside if marks >= 60:, write another if marks >= 75: print('B or above'). The inner if has extra indentation. Deep nesting is better handled by functions later.

A condition does not have to be a comparison. Python treats many values as truthy or falsy. Falsy values include False, None, 0, 0.0, '' (empty string), [] (empty list) and {} (empty dictionary). All other values are truthy. So if name: runs when name is a non-empty string. if 0: never runs its block.

items: Using = instead of == in a condition: if marks = 75: is a syntax error. Use if marks == 75:.
Forgetting the colon after if, elif or else: if marks >= 75 is a syntax error.
Wrong indentation: the block must be indented consistently; an unindented line after if is outside the block.
Putting a condition after else: else: is correct; else marks >= 60: is a syntax error.
Testing a range wrongly: marks >= 60 and <= 75 is invalid (Python does not repeat the left operand); write marks >= 60 and marks <= 75.

blocks.text: The if-elif-else chain is used in form validation, fee slabs, grade rules and menu choices. For repeated decisions, loops repeat the test. For reusable checks, move the rule into a function.

spec.title: if-elif-else for marks

examples.question: A college uses these grade rules for a Python course: marks ≥ 90 → A; marks ≥ 75 → B; marks ≥ 60 → C; otherwise D. The input marks is 78. Trace the if-elif-else tests in order, state the first true test, and give the output. Also give the grade code used by the check (A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4).
steps: Set marks = 78. The chain is: if marks >= 90: grade = 'A'; elif marks >= 75: grade = 'B'; elif marks >= 60: grade = 'C'; else: grade = 'D'.
Test 1: 78 >= 90. 78 is less than 90, so the result is False. Skip Grade A.
Test 2: 78 >= 75. 78 is 3 marks above 75, so the result is True. Run Grade B.
Because one branch has run, Python skips Test 3 (78 >= 60) and the else. Output is B.
Grade code: B is the second grade in A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, so code = 2.
examples.answer: The first true test is marks ≥ 75; the output is Grade B, with grade code 2.

traps: Using = in place of == is a syntax error; = assigns, == compares.
The first true branch wins. Reverse the order of 90 and 75, and marks 95 becomes B instead of A.
else takes no condition. else marks >= 60: is a syntax error; use elif marks >= 60:.
A missing colon after if, elif or else is a syntax error; the colon is part of the header.
Indentation defines the block. A line with the same indentation as if is outside the if, even if it looks related.

quiz.q: What does elif mean, and what punctuation ends every if, elif and else header?
quiz.a: elif means else if; every header ends with a colon (:).

quiz.q: Why does Python stop testing after the first True elif?
quiz.a: Only one branch should run; later tests cannot change the chosen block, so they are skipped.

quiz.q: marks = 82, rules 90 A, 75 B, 60 C, else D. What grade prints?
A student writes if marks >= 60: ... elif marks >= 90: ... else: ... For marks=95, what is wrong and what prints?
quiz.a: 95 >= 60 is True first, so it prints the ≥60 branch; the ≥90 test is never reached. Higher cut-offs must come first.

quiz.q: List three falsy values in Python.
What is the difference between = and ==?
quiz.a: = assigns a value; == compares two values and returns True or False.

quiz.q: Write a condition that is True when x is from 10 to 20 inclusive.
Why is if score > 50 or score < 100 not a useful test for scores 0 to 100?
quiz.a: Every score in 0..100 is either >50 or <100, so the condition is always True; use and for a range.

beyond: Not for the exam. Python's if-elif-else is the base for rule engines used in banking fraud checks and insurance premium slabs. Web frameworks route requests with condition chains, and data pipelines use them to clean rows before analysis. Newer curricula compare this with match-case, a pattern-matching statement added in Python 3.10. Search next for 'Python match case', 'guard clauses' and 'early return' to see how large programs keep decision chains short.
